lawyer:
Md Khalilur Rahman with Rubaiyat Hossain, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
None appears—For the Respondents.
parties:
Crescent Jute Mills Company Ltd ------ Petitioner 
Vs.  
Chairman, Khulna Labour Court & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This Rule Nisi was issued challenging the decision dated 5-3-1998 of the respondent No. 1, Khulna Labour Court Annexure C to the writ petition, allowing the Complaint Case No. C-13/1995 setting aside the order of dismissal of the respondent No. 2, Md Noor Hossain, from his service under the petitioner company, Crescent Jute Mills Company Ltd, with a direction to reinstate him with back wages. 

 2. The respondent No. 2 filed the aforesaid Complaint Case No. C-13/1995 under section 25(1)(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 in the Labour Court, Khulna stating that while he was discharging his duty to the satisfaction of all concerned allegation of misconduct was brought against him on 10-5-1994 and subsequently, he was placed under suspension on 23-11-1994 and charge-sheet was issued on 28-11-1994. The respondent No. 2 submitted his reply explaining his position. The petitioner thereafter did not take any step to have the allegation inquired into by appointing an inquiry officer or committee but it (petitioner) by letter dated 28-2-1995 dismissed the respondent No. 2 without providing any opportunity to the respondent No. 2 of being heard in the matter. The respondent No. 2 received the said order of dismissal on 1-3-1995 and submitted his grievance petition to the petitioner by registered post on 7-3-1995 with a prayer for his reinstatement but without any response, which compelled the respondent No. 2 to file the aforesaid case against the petitioner. 

 3. The petitioner contested the said Complaint Case by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the complaint petition alleging that the complaint case was not maintainable being barred by limitation and that the explanation submitted to the charge brought against the respondent No. 2 was not found satisfactory. Inquiry committee was, therefore, appointed. The respondent No. 2 was found guilty of the charge brought against him by the inquiry committee and during the inquiry the respondent No. 2 was given opportunity to defend himself before the inquiry committee. 

 4. In course of the hearing of the Complaint Case, the respondent No. 2 examined himself as PW 1 before the Labour Court and proved some documents and marked them as Exhibit 4. The petitioner, however, did not examine any witness nor produced and proved any documentary evidence in this case in support of its defence. PW 1 was, however, cross-examined on behalf of the petitioner before the Labour Court. 

 5. The Labour Court, in this background of the case, passed the impugned decision dated 5-3-1998 allowing the said Complaint Case of the respondent No. 2 with a direction on the petitioner to reinstate him with back wages on the finding that the respondent No. 2 succeeded in establishing his claim that the petitioner could not prove the charge of misconduct against him by initiating any inquiry into the charge by appointing any inquiry committee or inquiry officer but nonetheless, dismissed him from service by passing an order vide letter dated 25-5-1995. The Labour Court also found on the basis of evidence on record led by the respondent No. 2 that respondent No. 2 sent his grievance petition to the petitioner on 7-3-1995 under registered post and in this connection a copy of the grievance petition together with a copy of the postal receipt as well as a report from the Post Office to that effect were produced and proved and marked as Exhibits 4,4(1) and 5 respectively. 

 8. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman appearing with Ms Rubaiyat Hossain, submits that the impugned decision of the Labour Court is liable to be declared without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect on two grounds—firstly, the impugned decision is coram non judice, inasmuch as the case was not heard and disposed of by the Court which was constituted for the purpose as order No. 39 dated 26-2-1998 of the Labour Court showed that argument of both parties in the Complaint Case was heard in presence of the Chairman and another member, Nasu Mia, though Nasu Mia was never appointed as a member which seriously affected the validity of the impugned decision, and secondly, respondent No. 2 failed to prove that he sent his grievance petition to the petitioner company by registered post at all, inasmuch as the respondent No. 2 admitted in his complaint petition that he handed over the grievance petition to one Pulin Babu, Labour Officer of the petitioner company but he did not mention in his complaint petition that he sent the same by registered post. 

 9. We have heard the learned Lawyer for the petitioner and carefully perused the writ petition as well as the annexures thereto. We have also examined the record of the Complaint Case received from the Labour Court. It appears from the record that the respondent No. 2 produced and proved his grievance petition addressed to the petitioner company and the same was marked as Exhibit 4 . He also produced and proved a copy of the postal receipt and also the report from the concerned Postal Authority showing that the grievance petition was also sent to the petitioner company by registered post and the postal receipt as well as the said report of the postal authority were marked as Exts 4(1) and 5. The respondent No. 2 as PW 1 was cross-examined on behalf of the petitioner to the effect that the grievance petition as well as the postal receipt was not genuine and they were concocted which he categorically denied. The petitioner company did not adduce any evidence to substantiate its claim that the allegation of misconduct against the respondent No. 2 was enquired into and found correct by an inquiry committee and the respondent No. 2 did not send his grievance petition to the petitioner company under registered post. 

 10. It may be stated that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure as well as the Evidence Act are not applicable to any proceeding before the Labour Court in terms. The principle of these laws may be applied to any proceeding before a Labour Court insofar as it is necessary to conform to and uphold the principle of natural justice to avert any miscarriage of justice in any given case. 

 12. The contention of Mr Md Khalilur Rahman with regard to the Constitution of the Labour Court does not appear to be sound. We find from the order No. 26 dated 10-6-1997 of the Labour Court that it (Labour Court) was properly constituted with two members and the chairman to hear the case as required under law. It is also found from order No. 39 dated 26-2-1998 of the Labour Court that at the time of argument member Nasu Miah was absent. This position is also reflected in the impugned decision itself from the observation made therein by the Chairman of the Labour Court. No objection was raised by the petitioner company before the Labour Court as to the validity of the decision on the ground that Nasu Mia was not taken in as a member in course of the proceeding of the case. The impugned decision can, therefore, be regarded as a valid decision despite the fact that member Nasu Mia was absent when the argument was heard by the Labour Court in view of section 35(7) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969. Because absence of any member in course of hearing of a labour case will not affect the validity of the proceeding as well as the decision or award made by the Labour Court. 

 13. Mere assertion by the petitioner company before us that Nasu Mia was not appointed as a member of the Labour Court in relation to the present case without any valid proof will not render the impugned decision a nullity. This objection was not taken before the Labour Court nor it was taken in the writ petition filed before this Court. Whether said Nasu Mia was appointed as a member in course of the proceedings of the instant case in the event of valid absence or non-availability of a member originally appointed in the case is a question of fact. This question is raised now before us for the first time. In that view of the matter, we find that the impugned decision has been validly passed and it does not deserve any interference by this Court.
